claim_as_verified: At Google, about 1.5% of all test runs report a flaky result (John Micco, Google Testing Blog, 27 May 2016).
verbatim_quote: we see a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a "flaky" result
note: Flaky defined as a test that exhibits both a passing and a failing result with the same code.

claim_as_verified: Almost 16% of Google's tests have some level of flakiness (more than 1 in 7).
verbatim_quote: Almost 16% of our tests have some level of flakiness associated with them!
note: Same post also: 'If 1.5% of test results are flaky, 15 tests will likely fail' for a project of ~1000 tests.

claim_as_verified: Luo, Hariri, Eloussi, Marinov (FSE 2014) studied 201 commits that likely fix flaky tests in 51 open-source projects; root causes precisely classified for 161 of them.
verbatim_quote: We study in detail a total of 201 commits that likely fix flaky tests in 51 open-source projects.
note: 'We precisely classify the root causes for 161 commits'. Percentages below are of 161, not 201.

claim_as_verified: Top three root-cause categories: Async Wait 74/161 (45%), Concurrency 32/161 (20%), Test Order Dependency 19/161 (12%), together 77% of the 161.
verbatim_quote: 74 out of 161 (45%) commits are from the Async Wait category
note: Also: '32 out of 161 (20%) commits are from the Concurrency' and '19 out of 161 (12%) commits are from the Test Order' Dependency category; finding F.1 'The top three categories of flaky tests are Async Wait, Concurrency, and Test Order Dependency.'

claim_as_verified: Inozemtseva and Holmes (ICSE 2014) generated 31,000 test suites for five large Java systems (up to 724,000 LOC), measured statement, decision and modified condition coverage, and used mutation testing (mutants killed) as the effectiveness measure; correlation is low to moderate once suite size is controlled for, and stronger coverage types add no insight.
verbatim_quote: We found that there is a low to moderate correlation between coverage and effectiveness when the number of test cases in the suite is controlled for.
note: Conclusion: coverage 'should not be used as a quality target because it is not a good indicator of test suite effectiveness.' Authors were at University of Waterloo.

claim_as_verified: Google Testing Blog 'Code Coverage Best Practices' (Carlos Arguelles, Marko Ivankovic, Adam Bender, 7 Aug 2020): 60% acceptable, 75% commendable, 90% exemplary, as general guidelines, not mandates.
verbatim_quote: at Google we offer the general guidelines of 60% as "acceptable", 75% as "commendable" and 90% as "exemplary."
note: Preceded by 'Although there is no "ideal code coverage number,"' and followed by 'we like to stay away from broad top-down mandates'. Original uses curly quotes.

claim_as_verified: Petrovic and Ivankovic, 'State of Mutation Testing at Google' (ICSE SEIP 2018): diff-based probabilistic mutation analysis surfaced in code review, skipping uncovered and 'arid' lines; used by 6,000 engineers, affecting more than 14,000 code authors, processing about 30% of diffs with coverage.
verbatim_quote: The described system is used by 6,000 engineers in Google on all code changes they author or review

claim_as_verified: 'Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google' (Petrovic, Ivankovic, Fraser, Just; arXiv 2102.11378, Feb 2021; IEEE TSE 48(10), Oct 2022): mutates only changed code during code review, limits mutants per line (one per line) and per code review, selects operators by history; evaluated with more than 24,000 developers on more than 1,000 projects.
verbatim_quote: Mutation testing is done incrementally, mutating only changed code during code review, rather than the entire code base
note: Abstract also: 'limiting the number of mutants per line and per code review process'. TSE venue: DOI 10.1109/tse.2021.3107634 via Crossref.

claim_as_verified: In that paper, 82% of surfaced mutants that received feedback were labelled productive ('Please fix') by developers; productivity rose from 80% to 89% over time; initially developers classified 85% of reported mutants as unproductive (i.e. 15% productive before suppression heuristics).
verbatim_quote: 82% of all surfaced mutants with feedback were labeled as productive by developers.
note: Intro: heuristics 'improved the ratio of productive mutants from 15% to 89%'. Feedback via 'Please fix' / 'Not useful' links in Critique. Also: 87.5% of all generated mutants are killed by the tests.

claim_as_verified: 'Does mutation testing improve testing practices?' (Petrovic, Ivankovic, Fraser, Just; ICSE 2021) analysed almost 15 million mutants: developers exposed to mutants write more tests and improve suites so fewer mutants remain; mutants are coupled with real high-priority faults.
verbatim_quote: Our analyses suggest that developers using mutation testing write more tests, and actively improve their test suites with high quality tests such that fewer mutants remain.
note: Coupling: 'had mutation testing been used for the changes introducing the faults, it would have reported a live mutant that could have prevented the bug.'

claim_as_verified: Menzies, Nichols, Shull, Layman (Empirical Software Engineering, 2017; arXiv 1609.04886) tested the delayed issue effect on 171 software projects (2006--2014, Team Software Process data) and found no evidence for it.
verbatim_quote: We found no evidence for the delayed issue effect
note: Abstract: 'the effort to resolve issues in a later phase was not consistently or substantially greater than when issues were resolved soon after their introduction.' The study focuses on pre-delivery phases. EMSE journal year 2017 taken from the brief, arXiv says only 'Accepted with minor revisions to Journal of Empirical Software Engineering'.

claim_as_verified: The '100x' figure is stated in Boehm and Basili, 'Software Defect Reduction Top 10 List' (IEEE Computer, Jan 2001), item one, which itself softens it with 'often' and notes about 5:1 for small noncritical systems; the cost-escalation chart traces to Boehm's Software Engineering Economics (1981), and Menzies et al. say the effect was first reported in 1976.
verbatim_quote: Finding and fixing a software problem after delivery is often 100 times more expensive than finding and fixing it during the requirements and design phase.
note: Correction: the exact '100 times' wording is Boehm and Basili 2001, not a sentence verified in Boehm 1981 (book not checked). Same article: 'the cost-escalation factor for small, noncritical software systems to be more like 5:1 than 100:1.' Menzies et al. Fig. 1: 'A widely-recreated chart of the DIE effect. Adapted from Boehm'81', and 'The delayed issue effect was first reported in 1976'. Production (post-delivery) is the comparison, vs requirements/design.

claim_as_verified: Laurent Bossavit, 'The Leprechauns of Software Engineering: How folklore turns into fact and what to do about it' (Leanpub) has a chapter tracing the cost-of-defects curve.
verbatim_quote: Chapter 10: The cost of defects: an illustrated history
source_date: unknown (Leanpub, first published around 2012, not confirmed on the page)
note: Chapter subsections include 'Where's the data?', 'Theory-laden diagrams', 'Boehm's assent'. Publication year not confirmed from the page.

claim_as_verified: The test pyramid is usually credited to Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile (as the 'Test Automation Pyramid'); he drew it with Lisa Crispin in 2003--4 and described it at a scrum gathering in 2004. Fowler's TestPyramid bliki is dated 1 May 2012 (revised 7 Aug 2016 and 15 Nov 2017).
verbatim_quote: Most people know about the the Test Pyramid due to Mike Cohn, when he described it in his 2009 book Succeeding with Agile.
note: Fowler also notes Jason Huggins independently came up with the same idea around 2006. The doubled 'the the' is in the original.

claim_as_verified: Mike Wacker, 'Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests', Google Testing Blog, 22 Apr 2015: suggests a 70/20/10 split of unit, integration and end-to-end tests as a first guess.
verbatim_quote: As a good first guess, Google often suggests a 70/20/10 split: 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests, and 10% end-to-end tests.
note: Followed by 'The exact mix will be different for each team, but in general, it should retain that pyramid shape.'

claim_as_verified: Kent C. Dodds introduced the Testing Trophy in a tweet on 6 Feb 2018 (layers: Static, Unit, Integration, End to end); the post 'The Testing Trophy and Testing Classifications' is dated 3 June 2021. The phrase 'Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.' is Guillermo Rauch's tweet of 10 Dec 2016, which Dodds built on.
verbatim_quote: Guillermo Rauch @rauchg Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration. 4:43 PM (UTC) · December 10th, 2016
note: Original trophy tweet listed 'End to end w/ @Cypress_io', 'Integration & Unit w/ @fbjest', 'Static w/ @flowtype and @geteslint'; framed as 'A general guide for the **return on investment**'. Rauch tweet: x.com/rauchg/status/807626710350839808.

claim_as_verified: Meszaros (xUnit Test Patterns) defines five kinds of test double: dummy, fake, stub, spy, mock; as summarised by Fowler, only mocks insist on behaviour verification.
verbatim_quote: Dummy objects are passed around but never actually used. Usually they are just used to fill parameter lists.
note: Fowler: 'Fake objects actually have working implementations, but usually take some shortcut'; 'Stubs provide canned answers'; 'Spies are stubs that also record some information'; 'Mocks ... objects pre-programmed with expectations'. 'Of these kinds of doubles, only mocks insist upon behavior verification.' Book year 2007 (Addison-Wesley) not confirmed directly from a primary page here.

claim_as_verified: Fowler's 'Mocks Aren't Stubs' was first published 8 July 2004 and significantly revised 2 January 2007 to adopt Meszaros's vocabulary.
verbatim_quote: 08 July 2004: First published
note: Revision note: 'I also made various vocabulary changes to bring it into line with Gerard Meszaros's book of xunit patterns.'

claim_as_verified: Software Engineering at Google, chapter 13 'Test Doubles': prefer real implementations, then fakes; overuse of stubbing makes tests unclear and brittle; avoid interaction testing when possible.
verbatim_quote: A real implementation should be preferred over a test double. A fake is often the ideal solution if a real implementation can't be used in a test.
note: Section heading 'Prefer Realism Over Isolation'. Original uses a curly apostrophe in can't.

claim_as_verified: Software Engineering at Google, chapter 11 'Testing Overview': test sizes by resources, not scope: small tests run in a single process (often single thread), medium tests on a single machine (localhost), large tests anywhere (multiple machines).
verbatim_quote: small tests run in a single process, medium tests run on a single machine, and large tests run wherever they want
note: Sizes defined in chapter 11 (not 12). Reason given: 'the most important qualities we want from our test suite are speed and determinism, regardless of the scope of the test.'

claim_as_verified: Breck, Cai, Nielsen, Salib, Sculley (Google), 'The ML Test Score' (IEEE Big Data 2017): 28 specific tests and monitoring needs in four sections of seven: Tests for Features and Data, Tests for Model Development, Tests for ML Infrastructure, Monitoring Tests for ML. Half point per test run manually, full point if automated; final score is the minimum across the four sections.
verbatim_quote: In this paper, we present 28 specific tests and monitoring needs, drawn from experience with a wide range of production ML systems
note: PDF: https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/pubtools/4156.pdf ('c 2017 IEEE'). 'The final ML Test Score is computed by taking the minimum of the scores aggregated for each of the 4 sections.' Venue name IEEE Big Data inferred from copyright line plus common citation, not printed as such in the extracted text.

claim_as_verified: CheckList (Ribeiro, Wu, Guestrin, Singh, ACL 2020) has three test types: Minimum Functionality test (MFT), simple examples with labels like unit tests; Invariance test (INV), label-preserving perturbations where the prediction should not change; Directional Expectation test (DIR), perturbations where the label should change in a known direction.
verbatim_quote: An Invariance test (INV) is when we apply label-preserving perturbations to inputs and expect the model prediction to remain the same.
note: MFT: 'inspired by unit tests in software engineering, is a collection of simple examples (and labels) to check a behavior within a capability.' DIR: 'similar, except that the label is expected to change in a certain way.' INV and DIR are 'inspired by software metamorphic tests'. Title: 'Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList'.

claim_as_verified: Hypothesis current version is 6.168.3 (released 2026-09-28 on PyPI).
verbatim_quote: Hypothesis 6.168.3 documentation
note: Hypothesis releases very often; '6.168.x' is correct as of 2026-10-04.

claim_as_verified: Shrinking: Hypothesis minimises a failing test case and reports only the minimal failing test case; explicit @example cases are not shrunk.
verbatim_quote: The failing test case which has been fully shrunk (minimized) by Hypothesis. Hypothesis reports only the minimal failing test case to the user at the end of the test.
note: Glossary example: with assert n < 10, failing cases 921, 212, 10 are found; '10 is the minimal failing test case.'

claim_as_verified: Example database: failing test cases are saved and replayed; by default a DirectoryBasedExampleDatabase under .hypothesis/examples in the current working directory.
verbatim_quote: If not set, a DirectoryBasedExampleDatabase is created in the current working directory under .hypothesis/examples .
note: 'An instance of ExampleDatabase in which we will save failing test cases, and from which we will load previous failing test cases.' Docs suggest committing .hypothesis/examples only if Hypothesis version is pinned; a GitHubArtifactDatabase also exists.

claim_as_verified: settings.derandomize seeds Hypothesis from a hash of the test function so each run tests the same cases; default False, but True when running on CI.
verbatim_quote: The default is False . If running on CI, the default is True instead.
note: 'If True, seed Hypothesis' random number generator using a hash of the test function, so that every run will test the same set of test cases until you update Hypothesis, Python, or the test function.' The CI default is worth stating.

claim_as_verified: Stateful testing: RuleBasedStateMachine holds the system under test plus data (instance variables or Bundles); rules run in random applicable order and can change state or verify properties.
verbatim_quote: A RuleBasedStateMachine gives you a structured way to define state machines.
note: 'At any given point a random applicable rule will be executed.'

claim_as_verified: MacIver, Hatfield-Dodds et al., 'Hypothesis: A new approach to property-based testing', Journal of Open Source Software 4(43), 1891, 2019. Claessen and Hughes, 'QuickCheck: a lightweight tool for random testing of Haskell programs', ICFP 2000, pp. 268--279.
verbatim_quote: Hypothesis: A new approach to property-based testing
note: Metadata from Crossref. QuickCheck DOI 10.1145/351240.351266 (ICFP '00, Sept 2000).

claim_as_verified: pytest 8.4.0 (2025-06-02): async def tests now fail instead of warning and skipping when no suitable async plugin is installed (issue #11372).
verbatim_quote: Async tests will now fail, instead of warning+skipping, if you don't have any suitable plugin installed.

claim_as_verified: Pact is a code-first consumer-driven contract testing tool; the contract is generated while the consumer's automated tests run, so only the parts of the interaction the consumer actually uses get tested.
verbatim_quote: Pact is a code-first consumer-driven contract testing tool, and is generally used by developers and testers who code. The contract is generated during the execution of the automated consumer tests.
note: Also: 'Pact is a code-first tool for testing HTTP and message integrations using contract tests.'

claim_as_verified: pact-python current major version is 3 (3.4.1, released 2026-09-17).

claim_as_verified: concurrency: by default a new run replaces any pending run in the same group; cancel-in-progress: true also cancels the running one.

note: Docs also now describe an optional 'queue' property (single is default) to allow more than one pending run.

claim_as_verified: strategy.fail-fast applies to the whole matrix, defaults to true, and cancels all in-progress and queued matrix jobs when any one fails; continue-on-error applies per job.
verbatim_quote: GitHub will cancel all in-progress and queued jobs in the matrix if any job in the matrix fails. This property defaults to true .

claim_as_verified: Teknium (Nous Research, Sept 2026): Hermes Agent's main refactor run lasted about nineteen active hours, dispatched 1,393 subagents (218 at once), on a repository with more than a million lines of non-test Python (1,063,826 before, 698,363 after); non-test Python source fell 34.4%; estimated model cost about $19,300 for the main run, roughly $25k with follow-ups.
verbatim_quote: The main run lasted about nineteen active hours and dispatched 1,393 subagents, reaching 218 running at once.
note: Also: 'It reduced non-test Python source by 34.4%.' and 'The estimated model cost was about $19,300 for the main run, or roughly $25k including follow-up sessions. That excludes human review time.' Started Sept 2, PR merged Sept 4. Codebase split into 36 non-overlapping groups; workers used git worktrees; frozen test baseline used to judge failures. Inference ran on Claude Fable 5.1.

claim_as_verified: Community review caught regressions the tests missed: public names removed because nothing in the repo called them (external plugins could import them), and an automated rewrite of suppress() calls that changed exception handling at roughly 65 sites; fixed over two rounds of review before merge, with more fixes after merge.
verbatim_quote: These were real regressions the existing tests had missed.
note: Preceding sentences: 'Reviewers caught public names that workers had removed because they had no callers inside the repository, even though external plugins could import them. An automated rewrite of suppress() calls also changed exception handling at roughly 65 sites.' Follow-up: 'We also added a check that flags removed public names and tests for review.'

claim_as_verified: PyTorch docs: completely reproducible results are not guaranteed across PyTorch releases, individual commits, or platforms, and may differ between CPU and GPU even with identical seeds.
verbatim_quote: Completely reproducible results are not guaranteed across PyTorch releases, individual commits, or different platforms. Furthermore, results may not be reproducible between CPU and GPU executions, even when using identical seeds.
note: Includes 'individual commits' as well.

claim_as_verified: torch.use_deterministic_algorithms() makes PyTorch use deterministic algorithms where available and raise an error for ops known to be nondeterministic without a deterministic alternative.
verbatim_quote: torch.use_deterministic_algorithms() lets you configure PyTorch to use deterministic algorithms instead of nondeterministic ones where available, and to throw an error if an operation is known to be nondeterministic (and without a deterministic alternative).

claim_as_verified: Eugene Yan, 'How to Test Machine Learning Code and Systems' (Sep 2020) builds on Jeremy Jordan's 'Effective testing for machine learning systems': software tests check written logic, ML tests check learned logic; pre-train tests run without trained parameters, post-train tests check learned behaviour; plus evaluation.
verbatim_quote: Post-train tests check if the learned logic is expected.
note: Citation line on page: 'Yan, Ziyou. (Sep 2020).' Opens with 'Two weeks ago, Jeremy wrote a great post on Effective Testing for Machine Learning Systems.' Jordan's post: https://www.jeremyjordan.me/testing-ml/ . Jordan post dated 2020-08-19. The pre-train sentence in the original contains em-dashes, so a post-train quote is given.

claim_as_verified: Made With ML (Goku Mohandas, now 'by Anyscale') lesson 'Testing Machine Learning Systems: Code, Data and Models' covers pytest for code (assertions, parametrize, fixtures, markers, coverage), data tests with Great Expectations (expectations, suites, production), and model tests (training checks and CheckList-style behavioural tests: invariance, directional, minimum functionality), plus testing vs monitoring.
verbatim_quote: Learn how to test ML artifacts (code, data and models) to ensure a reliable ML system.

claim_as_verified: testcontainers (Python) current version 4.15.0 (2026-07-24); it starts real throwaway Docker containers (e.g. PostgresContainer('postgres:16')) for integration tests, so a Docker daemon is required.

claim_as_verified: vcrpy (current 8.3.0) has 4 record modes: once (default; replay, record only if no cassette file, error on new requests if cassette exists), new_episodes (replay old, record new), none (replay only, error on any new request), all (always record, never replay).
verbatim_quote: once is the default record mode, used when you do not set one.
note: none: 'The none record mode guarantees that no new HTTP requests will be made.' all: 'Record new interactions. Never replay previously recorded interactions.'

claim_as_verified: vcrpy filter_headers removes listed headers (e.g. authorization) from recorded cassettes so secrets are not committed; filter_query_parameters does the same for query strings.
verbatim_quote: Use the filter_headers configuration option with a list of headers to filter.
note: Example: use_cassette('test.yml', filter_headers=['authorization']).

claim_as_verified: pytest-recording (0.14.0, 2026-10-01) wraps VCR.py for pytest and defaults to the none record mode; set --record-mode=once (or other) to record; it adds a 'rewrite' mode and a block_network mark.

claim_as_verified: pytest-randomly (5.0.0) shuffles test order (by module, then class, then function), prints a seed reusable with --randomly-seed, and resets Python's global random.seed() to a fixed per-test value before each test's setup, run and teardown.
verbatim_quote: Pytest plugin to randomly order tests and control ``random.seed``.
note: README: 'Randomly shuffles the order of test items. This is done first at the level of modules, then at the level of test classes (if you have them), then at the order of functions.' The seed reset is derived from the base seed and the test ID.

claim_as_verified: pytest-rerunfailures (16.7) re-runs failing tests (e.g. --reruns 5, --reruns-delay, @pytest.mark.flaky) to eliminate intermittent failures.
verbatim_quote: pytest-rerunfailures is a plugin for pytest that re-runs tests to eliminate intermittent failures.
note: Original text has RST link markup around 'pytest'.
